Meeting header:
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, this is Alex from Redwood — I'm the AE on the account. We have Priya and Marco from our SE team. How's it going Jordan?
[00:08] Jordan Miles: Good, Alex, thanks. Ready to dig in. We mainly want to see the SDK flows and how auth and environment setup look, and confirm performance for payments use case.
[00:16] Sana Rodriguez: And some security questions up front — KMS, logs, data residency. Evan will jump in for that.
[00:22] Alex Chen: Perfect. We'll do a quick 10-15 minute walkthrough of the Python and TypeScript SDKs, show the Console quickstarts, then Priya will demo a local integration and provide tips for hosted vs dedicated.
[00:30] Summary (auto): quickstart + SDK integration overview; auth patterns (API keys, service accounts, SSO for Console); env setup; sample code; pilot next steps.
[00:40] Topics: SDK quickstart, auth, env vars, hosted vs dedicated, security/compliance, pilot scope.
---
Walkthrough and transcript body:
[02:00] Priya Patel: Ok, jumping into the Python quickstart. The fastest path is pip install redwood-inference (note: package name may vary in early docs), set REDWOOD_API_KEY as an env var, then from redwood import Client, call client.generate or client.chat. Example shown on the console quickstart.
[02:15] Sana Rodriguez: Sorry, can you repeat the exact env var name? We standardize names across our CI.
[02:18] Priya Patel: Yep — REDWOOD_API_KEY in upper case. For service integrations we also support setting up service accounts with scoped keys, which is better than using a personal key.
[02:30] Marco Li: For TypeScript it's similar: npm i @redwood/inference-sdk (again SDK names sometimes show differently in the docs), set process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY or use the Node SDK constructor with a key param. We have examples for serverless functions and for long-running workers in the repo.
[02:45] Jordan Miles: For our infra, we need to run some calls from serverless lambda-style functions and some from a dedicated microservice pool behind a VPC. How does auth and network look for those?
[02:58] Priya Patel: Great question. For hosted API calls from your functions you can call the public endpoint with the API key; if you want additional isolation you can use Redwood Dedicated which provisions a reserved pool and allows private VPC peering and private endpoints. That route uses mutual TLS or private links depending on cloud — we map it in the network diagram.
[03:18] Evan Park: On encryption — are request payloads encrypted in transit and at rest? What about key management?
[03:24] Marco Li: All traffic is TLS 1.2+ in transit. For hosted instances we manage keys; we can integrate with your KMS for Private deployments. For Dedicated you can bring-your-own-KMS (BYOK) and we also support HSM-backed keys for enterprise customers.
[03:38] Sana Rodriguez: How about audit logs and retention? We need logs for 12 months for PCI-related audits.
[03:43] Priya Patel: We export per-request traces and token-level cost breakdowns to your logging sink; retention and export are configurable. For Private deployments you control retention entirely. For hosted, we offer extended retention as an add-on. We'll share the compliance pack after the call.
[03:58] Alex Chen: Back to the SDK: Priya showed the chat and generate flows — remember that the SDK supports streaming responses for low-latency UI streams. In Python you can iterate over client.stream_chat to get tokens as they arrive.
[04:12] Priya Patel: Here's an example pseudo snippet — note, transcript auto-transcribed some code names incorrectly: 
[04:20] Priya Patel: "import redwood\nclient = redwood.Client(api_key=os.environ.get('REDWOOD_API_KEY'))\nresp = client.chat(messages=[{'role':'user','content':'summarize transaction 23847'}])\nprint(resp.text)"
[04:37] Sana Rodriguez: Do you have a managed SDK for rotating keys or will we need to build that ourselves?
[04:42] Marco Li: We provide short-lived service keys for CI/CD integrations and a key-rotation API. For SSO for the Console we integrate with SAML/SCIM for user sync and RBAC.
[04:52] Jordan Miles: On the topic of rate limits and batching — our flow will call generate for some high-volume endpoints. What's the best practice to manage cost vs latency?
[05:02] Priya Patel: Two levers: batching and prefix caching. For embeddings/upsert and high QPS, batch requests to the embeddings endpoint. For chat/generation, our runtime does continuous batching; on your side, keep request sizes small to avoid long tail latencies. Redwood Optimize will recommend batch sizes and quantization profiles based on your observed workload.
[05:22] Alex Chen: We'll run a short benchmark during the pilot to show token/sec and latency ranges on Hosted vs Dedicated. Typical numbers vary by model and sequence length — we'll include sample dashboards in the pilot.
[05:33] Sana Rodriguez: We have to confirm data residency — all credit card tokens must remain in US regions. Can you pin region?
[05:40] Priya Patel: For hosted we can pin region for your account; for Dedicated and Private you choose the region and we can restrict routing accordingly. We'll note that in the pilot scope.
[05:50] Jordan Miles: One thing — our devs want a quick local dev loop. How do we emulate the Console locally or use mock endpoints?
[05:56] Marco Li: We have a local mock server (redwood-mock) and a docker-compose example. For quickstart you can run the mock, set REDWOOD_API_URL to http://localhost:3000 and the SDK will hit that. That avoids sending real data to hosted infra while you iterate.
[06:12] Sana Rodriguez: Great. Anything special for TypeScript client auth in serverless — we use environment variables in Vercel and AWS Lambda.
[06:18] Priya Patel: Use ephemeral service keys for CI and environment variables for runtime. For Vercel, use encrypted project vars. For highly-sensitive environments, we recommend Dedicated + VPC peering to avoid public endpoints.
[06:30] Alex Chen: Let's walk quick through the Console — Marco, can you screen-share the quickstart?
[06:35] Marco Li: (screen share) Console shows API keys, sample curl, SDK snippets for Python/TS, a Routes view, and quick toggles to enable streaming or function/tool calling. We also have a Quickstart button that scaffolds a repo with sample code.
[06:50] Jordan Miles: The Quickstart scaffolding — can it generate a serverless function template for us?
[06:53] Marco Li: Yes, choose Node or Python and it will create a handler for the SDK, and a sample environment config including REDWOOD_API_KEY and REDWOOD_API_URL overrides.
[07:05] Sana Rodriguez: On monitoring — we need per-route latency SLOs and token-level cost dashboards; is that available in Redwood Console?
[07:12] Priya Patel: Yes, Console has per-route/model dashboards, token cost breakdown, and traces. You can export metrics to Prometheus or Datadog as well.
[07:22] Jordan Miles: For the pilot we want to try a 2-week benchmark with a small dedicated pool and compare to hosted baseline. Is that feasible?
[07:28] Alex Chen: Absolutely. Typical pilot: 2-week benchmarking, agreed set of prompts, and a simple success criteria doc. We'll provision sandbox keys and a small dedicated pool for the test.
[07:36] Evan Park: Legal will want a data flow and a list of sub-processors.
[07:40] Alex Chen: We'll include that in the security pack.
[07:43] Interrupt/crosstalk: [07:43] (short echo)
[07:45] Sana Rodriguez: A few quick nitty-gritty items — does the SDK support request tracing headers to connect with our distributed tracing?
[07:52] Marco Li: Yes, you can pass trace_id and Redwood will include it in console traces; we also export spans.
[07:58] Alex Chen: Any other blockers?
[08:00] Jordan Miles: Pricing — send us hosted vs dedicated estimates now, but the final ask will be unit economics for 1M requests/month with 2-second average response length.
[08:09] Alex Chen: Noted — we'll send the estimate.
[08:12] Closing recap (auto): Send pricing, share SOC2/compliance docs, provide SDK quickstart repo links and env examples, schedule pilot kickoff.
[08:20] Action recap on call: see action items in metadata.
[08:25] Alex Chen: Thanks everyone — Priya and Marco will follow up with the repo links and sample configs. We'll aim to get the pilot scoped and a kickoff scheduled for week of 11/9.
[08:34] Jordan Miles: Thanks, talk soon.

References / links mentioned: https://console.redwood.ai/quickstart (Console quickstart), https://docs.redwood.ai/sdk/python-quickstart, https://github.com/redwood-inference/quickstarts (sample repos)
